overview: Guadeloupe’s history spans Indigenous settlements, plantation slavery, repeated struggles for freedom and a continuing Caribbean society within France. This account focuses on the archipelago including Marie-Galante, Les Saintes and La Désirade. Historical administrative dependencies changed over time; they should not be confused with today’s territory.

periods.title: Pottery-using communities and stoneworking
periods.summary: The regional Early Ceramic Age spans approximately 500 BCE to 750 CE. Guadeloupe sites from this broad archaeological period contain stone tools, including rare volcanic-glass pieces; it is not the lifetime of a single state.

periods.title: French colonization
periods.summary: French colonists established themselves in 1635. The date marks European colonization, not the beginning of human life in the islands.

periods.title: British occupation
periods.summary: Britain occupied Guadeloupe in 1759; France regained it in 1763. These changes concerned colonial control.

periods.title: The first emancipation
periods.summary: The revolutionary abolition of 1794 took effect in Guadeloupe. Formerly enslaved people became legally free, before the violent reversal of 1802.

periods.title: Slavery is reimposed
periods.summary: French forces defeated resistance led by figures including Delgrès and Ignace. Bonaparte’s order of 16 July 1802 restored the old slaveholding legal order.

periods.title: Abolition and new political participation
periods.summary: Slavery was abolished in Guadeloupe on 27 May 1848. Legislative elections later that year brought formerly enslaved Louisy Mathieu into the National Assembly.

periods.title: Rebuilding after the 1928 cyclone
periods.summary: Ali Tur’s buildings at Lamentin formed part of Guadeloupe’s reconstruction. Reinforced concrete and Art Deco design reshaped public architecture.

periods.title: A French overseas department
periods.summary: The law of 19 March 1946 made Guadeloupe an overseas department. Its administrative territory still included the northern dependencies.

periods.title: The northern dependencies become separate collectivities
periods.summary: French Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy acquired separate overseas status in 2007, changing Guadeloupe’s administrative extent.

periods.title: International recognition of gwoka
periods.summary: UNESCO inscribed gwoka, recognizing a living practice of drumming, song, dance and communal participation.

items.text: At La Ramée in Sainte-Rose, hundreds of postholes form distinct concentrations. Archaeologists propose household areas within a late Cedrosan Saladoid village, while noting that individual building plans were not securely identified. The evidence supports organized settlement without supplying a complete house-by-house reconstruction.

At Bisdary-Yuiketi in Gourbeyre, an area beside a small settlement was interpreted as possible cultivation plots or gardens of the Cedrosan Saladoid period. The report called for further environmental and soil analysis. Recognizing a likely agricultural surface is different from identifying every crop grown there.

A 2024 study analyzed rare glassy artefacts from Guadeloupe and Dominica, including flakes and a core from Bisdary. Chemical analysis identified one genuine obsidian specimen with the Volcan du Tuf source on Basse-Terre. Its maker worked a difficult local material using a familiar stone-flaking method.

Most of the glass pieces instead proved to be unusual vitreous andesite. The researchers favour a volcanic origin, but had not located its deposit. Similarities to northern Martinique rocks suggest a research direction; they do not establish a proven trading route or the birthplace of every tool.

At L’Autre Bord in Le Moule, excavation revealed streets, houses, a well and an area used for butchery. Storm-deposited sand covered parts of the settlement, which researchers associate with destruction around 1760. These remains connect town life with water supply, food preparation and vulnerability to hurricanes.

Civil registration changed with legal status. After the first abolition, formerly enslaved people could enter ordinary civil registers; after re-enslavement, they were excluded again. Separate records for enslaved people later documented births, marriages and deaths. The organization of the archive itself preserves the effects of unequal law.

After 1848, special registers for newly free people recorded former registration numbers, given names, assigned surnames, birthplaces and residences. Entries can connect a family to a particular plantation. The departmental archives warn that many volumes were lost, especially in the 1918 Basse-Terre courthouse fire.

Legal historians Jean-François Niort and Jérémy Richard located the 1802 restoration order in the archives in 2008. The document had not appeared in the official law bulletin. Its recovery clarified how rights gained in 1794 were removed; it also separates Guadeloupe’s sequence from colonies where emancipation had never been implemented.

The 1848 parliamentary elections used universal male suffrage, leaving women outside the electorate. Victor Schœlcher was elected for both Martinique and Guadeloupe and chose the former, allowing Louisy Mathieu to take the Guadeloupe seat. Mathieu’s election linked emancipation with representation by a man who had experienced slavery.

Lamentin’s town centre preserves an ensemble by Ali Tur from the reconstruction after the 1928 cyclone. The regional inventory identifies reinforced-concrete structures, concrete roofs and simple Art Deco forms emphasizing vertical proportions. The buildings show how modern construction entered the public landscape during the 1930s.

In gwoka, a solo singer and responding chorus interact with ka drums and dancers. Participants form a circle, taking turns while the surrounding group claps and sings. Improvisation allows individual expression within a shared performance, making the audience part of the music’s social setting.

Families, friends, workshops and schools transmit both performance and drum-making skills. Gwoka accompanies celebrations and ordinary social life, as well as protest. Its UNESCO recognition in 2014 acknowledges a continuing practice whose musicians and dancers keep developing new forms.

Maryse Condé, born in Pointe-à-Pitre, became a novelist, playwright, critic and teacher whose career crossed the Caribbean, Africa, Europe and the United States. Columbia’s tribute describes how her teaching and public events helped broaden French literary study to include writing from many Francophone societies.

Condé’s novels include Hérémakhonon and Ségou. Her work and scholarship brought Caribbean and African histories, and women’s experience, into international literary discussion. Columbia colleagues remember this influence through both the books and the students and scholars she brought into conversation.

ending.text: Guadeloupe’s colonial administrative status changed to departmental status in 1946; it continues within France. Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy became separate collectivities in 2007. Neither transition ended Guadeloupean society or its cultural life.
